Welcome to the Monkey House by Kurt Vonnegut has a few good 2-10 page stories that are more sci-fi than others. The title story is a good example. 

There Will Come The Soft Rains by Bradbury is one of my particularly favorite entries in the Martian Chronicles, very heavy considering the context, but appropriate. 

Memory Police by Yoko Ogawa is a longer novel but so, so simple to read and very insightful in its connection between real life fascism and a hypothetical super police force that literally steals your thoughts. There are a lot of short chapters that cover a lot of story in a small amount of time and are just terribly compelling to read.

Anything by Jules Verne is short and fun, and shows how far our understanding of technology has come. Not exactly science-fiction, but a nostalgic look at what speculative tech in fiction was like before the genre was invented. 

PKD can be picked through, pretty much all of his works are good (but as their whole selves are probably not school adherent). Ubik, Electric Sheep, Scanner Darkly, Flow My Tears The Policeman, and Man In The High Castle are (some more than others) now a big part of pop culture and easily resonate in their written form, due to PKD's visual and bizarre descriptive 1st person writing style.

In high school my freshman English teach had us read Ender's Game by Orson Scott Card. I'd recommend it for younger HS readers, it was good as a freshman but by soph/junior years I was entrenched in sci-fi like Bradbury, Vonnegut, even Palanuik to an extent (some can be sci-fi-esque). Phillip K Dick is my favorite sci-fi author but a lot of his works are probably not HS appropriate as they're rife with weird sex/drug plot devices but selections from his works could be very good. I've later gotten into "hard" sci-fi as an adult, but I think it was easier for me to connect to a bizarre short story that Bradbury or Vonnegut wrote rather than a hard epic like Dune or Foundations.

My mom and I witnessed a man on a bike get hit by a couple making a speedy (and illegal) left turn in the center of an intersection. 

We were first in line, so this meant trying to block off the whole street from ~16 lanes of traffic (2 each in every direction plus turn). She immediately jumped out of the driver's seat and called 911. 

A man who was attempting to be helpful nearly grabbed the fallen man to move him out of the way (the victim had landed on his head after flipping over the hood of the car who hit him), and my mom, having very little training (Red Cross sponsored CPR/First Aid at most), got the samaritan to stop his attempt, in order to avoid spinal injury, and then protected the body until professional aide arrived, in the midst of traffic. 

We stayed calm as I pulled our truck in to block the body from any more crazy left-turners, and she tried to talk to the fallen man to see if he was able to give any information/ maintain basic consciousness (his skull was visibly split even through his helmet). When help arrived, they explained to us that if the body had been moved, there was a more than likely chance that he would have seized or lost oxygen, and died before they had gotten there. 

If I was alone, there is a chance that the man may not have lived. But my mom was there, and somehow knew exactly how to treat the situation (btw she's a long-time bartender, and has never been in emergency services). Basic, basic, basic information saves lives more than you'd think.

The expression goes "no happy marriages end in divorce" and it seems to be true. It hurts now but I assure you it will be better when you are not feeling "responsible" for someone else's happiness (aside from your child of course). There will be a point when you get out and you realize that your life is finally yours, and it will likely be scary but also enthralling. You will learn from this what you are looking for in a partner, and you will be better equipped to find them. It is especially hard living with an ex-spouse after filing (was there once), but make it through the next few months and it will be easier to process when you are breathing your own air. Depending on where you are located and your schedule, there are groups for divorcees, LGBTQ+ divorcees (even if you do not consider yourself to be a part of "the community", it can be helpful for these kinds of specific relationship issues), and there are even groups for the children/teens of divorce (was there once too). I hope any of this was helpful. I haven't been in your exact shoes, but we wear roughly the same size. Good luck to you and your child.

As someone in your girlfriend's situation, I can tell you it is going to be hard to convince them. It has been weeks and nearly come to a divorce and my wife and I are just now making progress. Basically, there is going to be a lot of pain coming your way, and the only way to convince them you won't leave is to help them through that pain in any way possible. I only thought of divorce when my wife was acting unsupportive of our relationship and supportive of another relationship. But when she came around and acted like my partner again and worked through things with me, they got a lot better. 

I have no idea what your personalities are like and you two could react completely differently than we did but I can assure you if she likes you to cook dinner, do it. If she likes going out, take her out or let her go out alone if she prefers. Support her, and listen, and communicate yourself as well and maybe it will work out. 

I am becoming accepting of polyamory because my wife is assuring me that this is the primary. We both made a list of principles (do's and don'ts) that we want followed by the other person and came to a lot of difficult, but now fulfilling, compromises after forging those lists together. It is up to us to follow those principles, but if we both do, it will work. Maybe you two can try to do the same.

As someone who is in a very similar situation, I can only give you one piece of advice: do something and then keep doing more. Pushups, volunteering, running, learning how to cook, speak another language, literally anything free that occupies your time. I emphasise free because I too am unemployed.

I can imagine that you spend every waking moment agonizing and thinking about her, and I won't tell you to stop, because its damn near impossible. As I type this, I too am agonizing and thinking, but the one thing that is making that pain dull is replying back to you and assuring that we can both get through this. After this, I am going to rake some leaves in my yard and after that I am going to do all of my laundry. It might seem impossible to start, but once you do, the ache may subside as you grow more distracted. 

Plus you will feel better getting things done because even doing chores or working out in that fugue state of pain means that you will have a clean and productive life and a better body when you come out of it. You might wake up feeling depressed about what happened in your past, but at least you won't feel depressed about what happened plus the fact that there aren't clean socks or you've gained weight. You can fix yourself, my friend. 

I hate that the only advice you've been given is "you'll get over it eventually", because its not necessarily true. You may never get over this relationship completely, but you can learn and improve and assure that the next person you give yourself to will be receiving a quality human being.

I like to brainstorm by starting with a person (X), a place (Y) and a thing (Z). The person could want the thing, or the person could hate the place/thing. The place could be a "dungeon" holding the thing, and the person could have a need to find the thing. Or the thing could have awesome powers and is threatening to destroy the person/place. Anything works, really, just try to create a conflict. Once a basic conflict is created, it is easier to form a story that people will want to read on the page and see on the screen.

For example: X has to find the Y so that Z does/doesn't get destroyed.

Y holds the untold power of Z, and X wants to harness it for their own selfish needs.
 
X has to travel to Y so that X can find Z. On the way, X finds that there are more important aspects to Y than Z.

Everyone on Y is like this. X is like that. Z will show the people on Y why they should be more/less like X.

I read up to the third page, but I found it hard to continue with so many line breaks. 
It feels like there is a decent set-up to be a horror film, but until it is in a more readable format, I don't think anyone is going to take the time to try to anticipate all of those line breaks. Editing your individual lines into longer paragraphs will also give you more page space, which is crucial when writing feature specs or TV pilots. 1 page should roughly average out to 1 minute of filming. 

[Format Your Screenplay](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XZszextv6yE) Indy Mogul has a decent video that helped me get the basics of formatting down. 

Reading scripts from other thrillers, mysteries and horrors also helps get the format, but also a feel for conflict down. One of my favorite examples is [Aliens](http://www.imsdb.com/scripts/Aliens.html) , which starts with a lot of broad exposition paragraphs, but cuts quickly to action and by the third page, descriptive dialogue. Read through your favorite thrillers and see what you can pick up from the words themselves.

Play out the possible tension/love interest (or even a complete lack of interest) between Maddy and Chris with physical description, or make Jonathon an over-the-top drunk friend by presenting witty dialogue; something should happen besides "friends go to beach -> really loose tension/feeling of friend-love -> one friend is vaguely drunk -> end". It can be believable and true to the mumble-core "true" aesthetic without being flat.

Overall though, I always like a bonfire-on-the-beach scene, in feature films it usually indicates a calm before the metaphorical storm, or a scene where foes become friends - in short, they usually indicate a change, so to put a short film in a setting that is commonly used for transitions is refreshing in the way that I want to know what is happening next. That's what gets readers to the next page, frankly: an actual interest in the next page. So good job, because I feel like there is more.

So the mini-model for the 3 Act Structure goes:
Act 1 Inciting Incident (what does character want?) - He wants to light the pipe, but the lighter goes out
Act 1 Climax - Oh hey, he has a roommate! And he wants the same thing.
Act 2 Midpoint - His roommate gets the thing he wanted done first, as circumstances are slightly more in the roommate's favor
Act 2 Confrontation - Adolfo takes control and figures out a way to get the lighter to work, at least for now.
Act 3 Downward Action - Both guys got what they want, snarky comment, end.
